items.title: Setting Up an Apache Virtual Host
items.text: This tutorial configures Apache to serve your Joomla site at /var/www/html/mySite using a custom local domain (e.g. mySite.local) instead of http://127.0.0.1/mySite.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Apache installed (part of your LAMP stack)
  • Joomla site already at /var/www/html/mySite
  • Root/sudo access

items.title: 1. Create the Virtual Host Config File
items.text:
sudo subl /etc/apache2/sites-available/mySite.conf

Paste the following:

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName mySite.local
    ServerAlias www.mySite.local
    DocumentRoot /var/www/html/mySite

    <Directory /var/www/html/mySite>
        Options Indexes FollowSymLinks
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>

    ErrorLog ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/mySite_error.log
    CustomLog ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/mySite_access.log combined
</VirtualHost>

AllowOverride All is important for Joomla, since it relies on .htaccess for SEF (search engine friendly) URLs.

items.title: 2. Enable the Site and Required Modules
items.text:
sudo a2ensite mySite.conf
sudo a2enmod rewrite

items.title: 3. Add the Local Domain to Hosts File
items.text:
sudo subl /etc/hosts

Add this line:

127.0.0.1   mySite.local www.mySite.local

items.title: 4. Restart Apache
items.text: sudo systemctl restart apache2

items.title: 5. Test It
items.text:
Open your browser and go to:

http://mySite.local

You should see your Joomla site load.

items.title: 6. Update Joomla's Site URL
items.text:
Joomla stores its base URL in the database. If you switch from http://127.0.0.1/mySite to http://mySite.local, update it:

  1. Log in to Joomla admin at http://mySite.local/administrator
  2. Go to System → Global Configuration
  3. Update the Site URL field (if present) — or check configuration.php in your Joomla root:
subl /var/www/html/mySite/configuration.php

Look for and update:

public $live_site = 'http://mySite.local';

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Issue Fix 403 Forbidden Check folder permissions: sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html/mySite .htaccess not working Confirm AllowOverride All and a2enmod rewrite was run Domain doesn't resolve Double-check /etc/hosts entry and clear browser DNS cache Apache won't restart Run sudo apache2ctl configtest to find syntax errors

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• If you're running multiple Joomla sites, repeat this process with a unique ServerName and .conf file per site.
  • Consider adding this vhost to Nginx Proxy Manager later if you want SSL or a reverse proxy in front of it.

items.text:

Octal Binary File Mode 0 000 --- 1 001 --x 2 010 -w- 3 011 -wx 4 100 r-- 5 101 r-x 6 110 rw- 7 111 rwx
  • Context Legend: u = user/owner, g = group, o = Other/wOrld
  • Permission Legend: r = read, w = write, x = execute

items.title: Quick Syntax Examples
items.text:
• u+x: Add execute permission for the owner
  • u-x: Remove execute permission from the owner
  • +x or a+x: Add execute permission for the owner, group, and world
  • o-rw: Remove read and write permission from anyone besides the owner and group owner
  • go=rw: Set the group owner and anyone besides the owner to have read and write permission
  • u+x,go=rx: Add execute permission for the owner and set the permissions for the group and others to read and execute

items.title: Copying Particles to existing theme
items.text:
This tutorial shows you the safe way to copy Gantry particles to your themes that won’t be overwritten again by theme updates.

A particle is made up of these things: * A Yaml file that tells Gantry 5 what fields the particle uses * A twig file that uses those fields to render output on your page * A scss file that contains the SASS/CSS to style the rendered particle on your page * One or more css/js files that contain JavaScript/CSS code to make the particle work.

Unzip the particles.zip package, navigate inside /particles/ folder then choose the particle or atom you wish to implement for your existing site then follow the steps below:

  • Copy particle_name.html.twig and particle_name.yaml to THEMENAME/custom/particles
  • Copy all js files (if any) to THEMENAME/custom/js and all css files (if any) to THEMENAME/custom/css
  • Copy _jlparticles.scss to THEMENAME/custom/scss.

Note: The _jlparticles.scss is global scss file for JoomLead particles.

The next thing you need to do is to ensure that the SCSS for the particle is loaded too. To do this, navigate in the directory structure to THEME_DIR/custom/scss and create a file called custom.scss if one doesn’t already exist.

If the /scss/ directory doesn’t exist within your custom folder, you will need to create that, too. If it already does, just open it and make your additions/changes directly to the file.

Open custom.scss file then add

@import "dependencies";
@import "jlparticles";

Go to the base outline Styles tab and Hit Recompile CSS button in the upper right corner.

items.title: Installing the LAMP Stack with MariaDB on Linux
items.text: LAMP stands for Linux, Apache, MariaDB, and PHP. This tutorial walks you through installing and configuring a full LAMP stack on Ubuntu or Linux Mint.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A system running Ubuntu 22.04+ or Linux Mint 22.x
  • A user account with sudo privileges
  • An internet connection

items.title: Step 1: Update Your System
items.text:
Before installing anything, make sure your package list and installed packages are up to date.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

items.title: Step 2: Install Apache
items.text:
Apache is the web server that will serve your web content.

sudo apt install apache2 -y

items.title: Verify Apache is running
items.text:
sudo systemctl status apache2

You should see active (running) in the output. You can also open a browser and navigate to http://127.0.0.1/ — you should see the default Apache welcome page.

items.title: Enable Apache to start on boot
items.text: sudo systemctl enable apache2

items.title: Step 3: Install MariaDB
items.text:
MariaDB is a community-developed fork of MySQL and is fully compatible with it.

sudo apt install mariadb-server mariadb-client -y

items.title: Start and enable MariaDB
items.text:
sudo systemctl start mariadb
sudo systemctl enable mariadb

items.title: Secure the MariaDB installation
items.text:
Run the included security script to set a root password, remove anonymous users, and disable remote root login.

sudo mysql_secure_installation

You will be prompted with a series of questions. Recommended answers:

Prompt Recommended Answer Switch to unix_socket authentication? N Change the root password? Y (set a strong password) Remove anonymous users? Y Disallow root login remotely? Y Remove test database? Y Reload privilege tables? Y

items.title: Verify MariaDB is running
items.text: sudo systemctl status mariadb

items.title: Log in to MariaDB
items.text:
sudo mariadb -u root -p

Enter your root password when prompted. Once inside, you can exit with:

EXIT;

items.title: Step 4: Install PHP
items.text:
PHP is the server-side scripting language that connects Apache and MariaDB together.

sudo apt install php libapache2-mod-php php-mysql -y

items.title: Useful additional PHP extensions
items.text:
These are commonly needed for web applications like WordPress, Joomla, etc.:

sudo apt install php-curl php-gd php-mbstring php-xml php-zip php-intl php-bcmath -y

items.title: Verify PHP is installed
items.text: php -v

items.title: Step 5: Configure Apache to Prefer PHP Files
items.text:
By default, Apache serves index.html before index.php. To change this:

sudo subl /etc/apache2/mods-enabled/dir.conf

Find the DirectoryIndex line and move index.php to the front:

DirectoryIndex index.php index.html index.cgi index.pl index.xhtml index.htm

Save the file, then restart Apache:

sudo systemctl restart apache2

items.title: Step 6: Test PHP
items.text:
Create a test PHP file in the web root:

sudo subl /var/www/html/info.php

Add the following content:

<?php
phpinfo();
?>

Save the file and open http://127.0.0.1/info.php in your browser. You should see a detailed PHP information page.

⚠️ Security note: Delete this file once you've confirmed PHP is working.

sudo rm /var/www/html/info.php

items.title: Step 7: Create a Database and User (Optional but Recommended)
items.text:
Rather than using the root account for your applications, create a dedicated database and user.

sudo mariadb -u root -p

Inside the MariaDB shell:

CREATE DATABASE myapp_db;
CREATE USER 'myapp_user'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'your_strong_password';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON myapp_db.* TO 'myapp_user'@'localhost';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
EXIT;

items.title: Step 8: Configure Apache Virtual Hosts (Optional)
items.text:
If you plan to run multiple sites, set up a virtual host for each one. Your web files live in /var/www/html/.

Create a new virtual host config:

sudo subl /etc/apache2/sites-available/mysite.conf

Add the following (adjust as needed):

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName mysite.local
    ServerAdmin webmaster@localhost
    DocumentRoot /var/www/html/mysite

    <Directory /var/www/html/mysite>
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>

    ErrorLog ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/mysite_error.log
    CustomLog ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/mysite_access.log combined
</VirtualHost>

Enable the site and the rewrite module, then reload Apache:

sudo a2ensite mysite.conf
sudo a2enmod rewrite
sudo systemctl reload apache2

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Component Package Service Web Server apache2 apache2 Database mariadb-server mariadb PHP php libapache2-mod-php php-mysql (handled by Apache)

Your LAMP stack is now installed and ready to use. Web files go in /var/www/html/, and you can manage your databases via sudo mariadb -u root -p.

items.title: Quick Reference: Useful Commands
items.text:
# Apache
sudo systemctl start|stop|restart|reload|status apache2

# MariaDB
sudo systemctl start|stop|restart|status mariadb
sudo mariadb -u root -p

# Check Apache config for errors
sudo apache2ctl configtest

# Enable/disable Apache modules
sudo a2enmod <module>
sudo a2dismod <module>

# Enable/disable Apache sites
sudo a2ensite <site>.conf
sudo a2dissite <site>.conf

items.title: 1. Beginning Phase
items.text:
• Untap Step – Active player untaps all their tapped permanents (no priority, no players act)
  • Upkeep Step – Triggered abilities that occur "at the beginning of upkeep" go on the stack; players get priority
  • Draw Step – Active player draws a card; players get priority

items.title: 2. Precombat Main Phase
items.text: • Single step – play lands, cast sorcery-speed spells, activate abilities

items.title: 3. Combat Phase
items.text:
• Beginning of Combat Step – last chance to act before attackers are declared
  • Declare Attackers Step – active player declares attackers; attacking creatures tap (unless they have vigilance)
  • Declare Blockers Step – defending player declares blockers
  • Combat Damage Step – combat damage is assigned and dealt (repeats if any attacker/blocker has first strike or double strike)
  • End of Combat Step – last chance to act before combat ends

items.title: 4. Postcombat Main Phase
items.text: • Single step – same as precombat main phase, play remaining spells/lands

items.title: 5. Ending Phase
items.text:
• End Step – triggered abilities that occur "at the beginning of the end step" go on the stack
  • Cleanup Step – active player discards down to maximum hand size (usually 7), damage is removed from permanents, "until end of turn" effects end (no priority given unless a trigger happens)

items.title: It uses the Scryfall API to fetch MTG card images.
JavaScript
items.text:
$(document).ready(function () {
    $(".card-link").hover(function () {
        var cardName = $(this).data("card-name");
        var apiUrl = "https://api.scryfall.com/cards/named?fuzzy=" + encodeURIComponent(cardName);

        $.get(apiUrl, function (data) {
            var cardTooltip = $(".card-tooltip");
            var imageUrl = "";

            // Check if it's a single-faced card
            if (data.image_uris) {
                imageUrl = data.image_uris.normal;
            } 
            // If not, it's likely a double-faced/modal card; get the front face
            else if (data.card_faces && data.card_faces[0].image_uris) {
                imageUrl = data.card_faces[0].image_uris.normal;
            }

            if (imageUrl) {
                cardTooltip.find(".card-tooltip-content").html(
                    "<img src='" + imageUrl + "' alt='" + cardName + "' style='max-width: 300px; display: block;'>"
                );
                cardTooltip.show();
            }
        });
    }, function () {
        // Keep visible on mouse out
    });

    $(document).on("click", function (e) {
        if (!$(e.target).closest(".card-link").length) {
            $(".card-tooltip").hide();
        }
    });
});

items.title: Command Line Interface (CLI)
items.text:
cd /path/to/your/zensical/

python3 -m venv .venv 
# this creates a hidden directory named .venv inside
# your project folder containing a isolated copy of the Python binary and pip.
source .venv/bin/activate

zensical serve # Live update server at http://127.0.0.1:8000/zensical/site/
zensical build

deactivate # exit the virtual environment (venv)
 #

items.title: Commands
items.text:
• zensical new [dir-name] - Create a new project.
  • zensical serve - Start the live-reloading docs server.
  • zensical build - Build the documentation site.
  • zensical -h - Print help message and exit.
